- Base URL: https://api.tally.so

| 400 | Bad Request - The request was malformed or contained invalid parameters |

Wondering what you can create with Tally’s API? Here’s what our developer community has built with early access to the API:
1. Dynamic Form Creation & Customization
- Programmatically create forms
- Duplicate and personalize a form for a new client; to do so fetch an existing form's structure, then create a new one from it:
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{ "status": "PUBLISHED", "blocks": [ { "uuid": "<title-block-uuid>", "type": "FORM_TITLE", "payload": { "title": "Client Intake – Acme Co" } }, ...copied from GET /forms/{formId} ] }'
status is required ("PUBLISHED", or "DRAFT"/blank for a draft). There's no name field, the API ignores it. The form's name comes from its first block, which must be a FORM_TITLE block whose payload.title becomes the form name.
2. Real-Time Form Updates
- Enable/disable fields based on business rules or time
- Dynamically change field visibility or values
- Auto-update dropdown options from live data sources (e.g. Notion, Airtable, Google Sheets); to do so pull the latest values from your source, then push them into the form's block schema:
# 1. Fetch the full form — you need every block, not just the dropdown
curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
# 2. Each dropdown choice is its own DROPDOWN_OPTION block, sharing a
#    groupUuid with the DROPDOWN block. Update the ones you need:
#    { "uuid": "<option-uuid>", "type": "DROPDOWN_OPTION", "groupUuid": "<dropdown-group-uuid>", "payload": { "text": "Option A" } }
# 3. PATCH back the ENTIRE blocks array — PATCH replaces the whole set,
#    so any block you leave out gets deleted
curl --request PATCH \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{ "blocks": [ ...full blocks array from step 1, with the DROPDOWN_OPTION blocks updated... ] }'
Always GET the form first and PATCH back the complete 
blocks array — partial updates will delete any block you don't include. See the Block Schema Reference for the full dropdown-option block shape.
3. Data Access & Management
- Filter and sync submissions into external tools (CRMs, dashboards, databases), to do so list new submissions and forward them downstream:
curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId}/submissions \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
Or use a webhook instead of polling — you'll get each submission pushed to your endpoint the moment it's created, without counting against your rate limit.
- Delete submissions programmatically
curl --request DELETE \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId}/submissions/{submissionId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
Returns 
204 on success. Deleted submissions move to Trash and follow the same recovery window as manual deletion.
Is the Tally API free?
Yes, the Tally API is free for all Tally users, including the free plan. No paid plan required to get started.
What can I build with the Tally API?
You can programmatically create and manage forms, update fields dynamically, fetch and delete submissions, and sync data with external tools like Notion, Airtable, Google Sheets, or your own database. Can I use the Tally API with Make, n8n, or Zapier?
Yes. The Tally API works great alongside no-code automation tools. Use it to create or update forms dynamically, then route submission data through your automation stack. Many users combine the API with Make or n8n to build end-to-end workflows.
How do I authenticate with the Tally API?
The Tally API uses token-based authentication. Find your API key in your account settings and include it as a Bearer token in your request headers. Full details in the developer docs.
Does Tally have webhooks or just an API?
Tally has both. Webhooks push data to your tools automatically when a form is submitted. The API gives you full programmatic control — create forms, manage submissions, update fields, and more. Many users use both together.
Can I create forms programmatically and prefill fields?
Yes, you can create forms via the API and dynamically set field values, making it easy to personalise forms per user, event, or client without manual setup.
Is there a rate limit on the API? Yes — 100 requests per minute. If you're syncing submissions continuously, use a webhook instead of polling so you don't hit it.

Discover 10 free consent form templates you can use in Tally.","content":"If you offer services or activities that involve risk, or if your company needs permission to use content like photos, videos, or personal information, consent forms help you get clear approval upfront. Organizations and groups doing research also use consent forms so participants understand what they're agreeing to.
A good consent form template explains exactly what you're asking permission for and how information will be used. 
Keep in mind that consent requirements vary by location and industry, especially if you're collecting health information, working with minors, or operating in regulated sectors. It's worth checking relevant local and national laws to make sure your forms meet your specific requirements.
Find 10 free consent form templates below
A consent form documents permission before using someone's information, image, or involving them in activities that carry risk or require disclosure. These forms protect both parties by clearly outlining what's being agreed to, like photo usage rights or participation in research studies or physical activities.
Most consent forms capture essential details like contact information, specific permissions being granted, and any relevant health or safety considerations. They also include clear language about how information will be used and stored, plus an easy way for people to withdraw their consent later.
Consent forms help ensure everyone understands what they're agreeing to upfront, which prevents misunderstandings and protects your organization or brand from potential liability down the line.
Consent forms aren't one-size-fits-all. The type you need depends on your activity, who's involved, and what permissions you're seeking. Some situations call for detailed documentation, while others just need simple agreement. Here are the main types and when you'd typically use them.
These are for research and studies where people need complete understanding before deciding to participate. Think university research, surveys with sensitive topics, or any formal data collection where participants should understand exactly what they're agreeing to.
When you need to share someone's information with other companies or partners, these forms keep things transparent. They're particularly helpful for staying compliant with privacy laws while being upfront about how data gets used and protected.
Cover situations where you're capturing photos, audio, or video content. Whether it's for professional photography, training sessions, interviews, or marketing materials, they set clear expectations about how the content will be used and where it might appear.
Used when businesses want to post content featuring customers, employees, or event participants on their social channels. They address platform-specific considerations like how the participant would like to be identified, content duration, and which social networks will be used.
Great for podcasters, journalists, and content creators who need clear permission to quote, publish, or share interview material. They address things like editing rights and how people want to be credited.
Required when children are involved in activities beyond regular school requirements. These parental consent forms cover safety, medical information, and emergency contacts and inform parents what their child will be doing.
Perfect for hands-on experiences that involves tools, equipment, or physical activity. They gather information about respondents’ medical conditions and physical limitations while addressing safety risks and liability concerns.
Whether you need permission for recordings, data sharing, or participant activities, consent forms help you collect clear agreements. Every situation requiring consent is different and often needs more than just a simple checkbox, that's why we've created templates for the most common consent scenarios. Each template is free, ready to use, and easy to customize to fit your specific business or project.
An informed consent form helps researchers collect consent from study participants. These forms are used for academic researchers, market research companies, and organizations conducting formal studies where participants need to understand what they're agreeing to.
This type of consent form walks participants through study details step by step, covering procedures, time commitments, risks and benefits, and their rights.
The key areas covered in informed consent forms are:
- Study overview with researcher contact information
- Explanation of activities and time requirements
- Risk and benefit disclosure
- Privacy and data protection measures
- Specific consent statements that participants must acknowledge
- Digital signature
You’ll find this type of consent form is often required before starting research activities to help protect both participants and researchers because it ensures ethical standards are met and makes it clear what participants are agreeing to and how they can withdraw.
A data sharing consent form collects permission before sharing customer information with third parties. These forms are useful for companies working with payment processors, delivery services, marketing partners, or any situation where customer data needs to leave your organization to provide services.
The key areas to cover in data sharing consent forms are:
- Clear organization details and contact information
- Specific explanation of what data needs to be shared
- Who will receive the information and why
- How the third party will use the data
- Consent statements that customers must actively agree to
- Easy withdrawal process
This type of consent form clearly explains what information you want to share, who will receive it, and exactly how it will be used.  
A photo release form collects permission before using someone's image in your photos or videos. Photographers rely on these for commercial shoots with models and subjects, and stock photo companies typically require them before accepting submissions that feature people.
These forms describe exactly how images will be used, from marketing materials to social media, so everyone knows what they're agreeing to upfront.
The key areas to cover in a photo release form are:
- Contact details and identification
- Specific usage rights you're requesting
- Whether you can use their name or tag them online
- Permission for identifiable vs. non-identifiable use
- Digital signature for legal protection
You can also customize this template for location releases when shooting at private buildings or distinctive properties that need permission.
A recording consent form gets clear permission before capturing audio or video that you plan to share publicly or use in marketing materials. Content creators and podcasters rely on these for legal protection. Customer experience teams might also use them when they want to feature customer conversations in testimonials or case studies.
The key areas to cover in a recording consent form are:
- Clear explanation of what's being recorded and why
- Specific details about how the recording will be used and shared
- Confirmation that participants can stop recording anytime
- Contact information for questions
- Digital signature for documentation
This type of consent form is essential when recordings might appear in company marketing materials, on websites, or in published content. It's different from interview consent forms, which typically cover internal research while this one focuses on public use and sharing.
A social media consent form collects permission before posting photos, videos, or content featuring people on your social channels and marketing materials. Marketing teams use these when featuring customers or employees in campaigns to confirm consent and check how participants want to be identified if their likeness is used online or in print.
The key areas to cover in a social media consent form are:
- Clear explanation of how photos and videos will be used
- Specific platforms and channels where content may appear
- Whether people can be tagged or identified by name
- Confirmation that content may be edited or adapted
- Easy opt-out process for withdrawing consent
Social media consent forms work well for businesses posting customer showcases or content featuring employees, community organizations sharing member highlights, or any situation where you're capturing content featuring people that might go public. Unlike large events that typically already include consent in ticket terms, these forms give you direct permission for specific social media use.
A client marketing consent form helps service providers get permission to share client results, progress photos, testimonials, and success stories in their marketing. Personal trainers, coaches, consultants, and freelancers use these to showcase their work while giving clients control over what gets shared and how they're identified.
The key areas to cover in a client marketing consent form are:
- Clear explanation of why you want to share client content
- Specific types of content you might post (photos, messages, testimonials)
- Multiple privacy levels for each content type
- Options to be tagged, stay anonymous, or require case-by-case approval
- Personal, honest tone that builds trust
Client marketing consent forms are useful for service-based businesses that want to feature their client results over time, not just single events or photos.
An interview consent form gets permission to record and document interviews for research, reporting, or internal organizational use. Market researchers and HR teams use these when conducting studies, but journalists also rely on them for background interviews that won't be published immediately.
This form focuses on internal documentation rather than public sharing, with strong privacy protections built in.
The key areas to cover in an interview consent form are:
- Clear explanation of how recordings will be used internally
- Strong confidentiality and data handling commitments
- Emphasis on voluntary participation and right to withdraw
- Options for audio, video, or notes-only documentation
- Choice of how the person wants to be identified
- Formal consent confirmation process
Interview consent forms work well for research studies, internal company interviews, background journalism, or any situation where you need detailed documentation with privacy protections. They're more comprehensive than simple recording forms since they often involve sensitive topics or proprietary information.
A parental consent form collects permission from parents before children participate in activities, field trips, or programs outside regular requirements. Schools and camps use these for excursions and special events. Youth sports teams, after-school programs, and community organizations might also use them for activities.
This form gathers essential safety details and emergency contacts beyond basic permission. The key areas to cover in a parental consent form are:
- Complete child and parent/guardian information
- Medical conditions, allergies, and special requirements
- Emergency contact details if parents aren't reachable
- Clear activity description and associated risks
- Permission for emergency medical treatment
- Liability release and financial responsibility acknowledgment
Parental consent forms protect both the organization and ensure parents understand what their child will be doing, potential risks involved, and that proper medical information is available if needed.
A liability waiver and release form protects businesses from legal claims when customers participate in potentially risky activities. Free for all Tally users, no coding needed","content":"Conditional logic lets your form adapt in real time based on how someone answers. Show or hide questions, skip irrelevant pages, jump to a custom thank you page, or route respondents down a completely different path — all based on their responses. The result is a smarter, shorter form that feels personal instead of generic.
Conditional logic in Tally is completely free to use. No upgrade needed, no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
Conditional logic is a versatile tool that allows you to create tailored form experiences based on user responses. Some examples of using conditional logic include:
- Progressive disclosure: Only show fields when they're needed. Use this for waiting list forms, client check-in forms, or any form where follow-up questions depend on a previous answer.
- Lead qualification: Ask progressively detailed questions and end the form early if someone doesn't qualify — no wasted time for you or them. Route high-intent leads to a specific page or redirect URL.
- Pricing calculators: Use calculated fields with conditional logic to display custom quotes, totals, or estimates based on selections — updated live as respondents answer.
- Personalized confirmation: Show a different thank you page or message based on how someone answered — useful for quiz results, NPS follow-ups, or application outcomes.
- Personality quizzes: Display the result category respondents scored highest on, using calculated fields and conditional page jumps. See how in the personality quiz guide.

/logic to add conditional logic to your form. You can add conditions on any type of input block. Click 
: next to the logic block to remove, duplicate, add new, or wrap conditions in a group.

cmd/ctrl + shift + L shortcut to add a conditional logic block under a selected input block.

When dropdown to choose how they're combined. - When all match: every condition must be true (an AND rule). Use this to narrow down to a specific combination of answers, for example, respondents from "Germany" who are older than 18.
- When any match: at least one condition must be true (an OR rule). Use this when several different answers should trigger the same result, for example, someone who selected "Consulting" or "Freelance" as their job type.

When dealing with long forms, conditional logic can become more intricate and prone to logical errors. With extensive fields, conditions, and actions, it's crucial to be cautious, as even small mistakes can sneak in. To effectively troubleshoot your form, you can follow these general steps:
- Review the conditional logic blocks: Start by carefully examining the conditional logic rules you've set up for your form. Check if the conditions are linked to the correct fields and actions. Ensure that you have configured the logic correctly based on your specific requirements.
- Edit field names: Replace the default question field names with descriptive titles that accurately describe the question or information being collected. This will make it easier to identify and manage fields when setting up or troubleshooting conditional logic.
- Test your form: Before sending your form to respondents, test different scenarios. You may find it easier to spot any errors by doing several test runs and selecting different answer options each time.
- Use @ mentions to identify the specific issue: By strategically placing @ mentions before or after the conditional logic block, you create a mechanism to track the values of relevant inputs and calculated fields at specific points in the form's execution.
- Simplify to narrow down the problem: By reducing the complexity of the logic, you can isolate specific conditions or actions that may be causing the issue and focus your efforts on debugging those areas.
What is a conditional logic form?
A conditional logic form is a form that dynamically changes based on how someone answers. Using IF/THEN rules, you can show, hide, or skip questions so each respondent only sees what's relevant to them.
Is Tally's conditional logic free?
Yes. Conditional logic is available for free to all Tally users. There are no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
What types of actions can I trigger with conditional logic?
Tally supports six actions: Jump to page, Calculate a value, Make answers required, Show or hide blocks, Hide button to disable completion, and Redirect to different URLs.
Can I combine conditional logic with multi-step forms?
Absolutely. Conditional logic and multi-step forms work great together. You can skip entire pages, show different paths based on answers, and create personalized form flows.
Why isn't my conditional logic working?
The most common issues are: the logic block is placed on the wrong page, conditions reference the wrong field, or the form hasn't been tested with all answer combinations. Free for all users.","content":"You can use URL parameters to pass data into hidden fields in your form. Free and easy to set up today.","content":"Calculated fields let you perform automatic calculations inside your form — think pricing calculators, quiz score totals, or lead scoring, all based on respondents' answers. You can use simple numeric and text operations, or write full formula expressions for more advanced logic.
Calculated fields are available for free to all Tally users. 
Calculated fields enable you to dynamically calculate values based on respondents' answers. Here are some common use cases for calculated fields:
- Pricing calculators: Build a checkout form where the total updates live as respondents choose products, quantities, or add-ons. Feed the result directly into a payment block.
- Quiz scoring: Add points per correct answer and show respondents their final score on a thank you page. See our guide to building scored quizzes.
- Personality and category quizzes: Tally up answers across categories and route respondents to the matching result page. See our personality quiz guide.
- Lead qualification: Assign a score or status label ("Hot lead," "Nurture") based on the answers someone gives, and sync it to your CRM via an integration.
- Name and text concatenation: Combine first name and last name into a single "Full name" field, or build a custom reference string from multiple inputs.
- Conditional redirects that use a calculated field with conditional logic to redirect respondents to different pages based on their responses.
Insert a calculated field in your form by typing 
/calculated field. In most cases, it’s best to add calculated fields on top of the form.
- Name your calculated field to easily retrieve it in calculations later on
- Choose whether the value will be text or a numeric value (number)
- Then, add an initial value as a starting point of your calculation. You can type a value, leave it blank or select a value from the dropdown.
Before determining the value of a calculated field, you need to add conditional logic to your form. Type
/logic to insert it below your calculated field block. Only you can see the calculated field and conditional logic blocks, respondents won’t see them on your published form. Conditional logic allows you to perform multiple actions. When using calculated fields, you want to select the 
Calculate action.
You can perform several numeric and textual operations with the 
Calculate action:
- Add a value
- Subtract a value
- Multiply with a value
- Divide with a value
- Assign: add a text value, for example, a label or a status, to sync contacts from your form submissions with a CRM or another tool or assign a category name to respondents based on their selected answers. Respondents won’t see this information unless it’s mentioned elsewhere in the form.
- Concatenate values: combine values in one string. For example, if you have fields for first name and last name in your form, you can create a calculated field that combines the values entered in these two fields into a single ‘Full name’ field. To use this, you need to select Text when creating a calculated field.
With formulas you write a single expression to combine multiple operations in one go, instead of chaining separate logic steps. Reference any field with 
@ mentions (e.g. (@price * @quantity) - @discount) and get real-time validation as you type.
Supported operations are 
+ - * / and parentheses ( ) for grouping
| Use case | Formula | 
| Add tax (5%) | @price × 1.05 | 
| Total with quantity | @price × @quantity | 
| Price after discount | (@price × @quantity) - @discount | 
| Apply a dynamic discount % (discount set by respondent) | @price × ((100 − @discount) / 100) | 
| Apply a fixed discount % (e.g. always 20% off) | @price × ((100 − 20) / 100) | 
| Remove a dynamic tax rate from a total (tax rate set by respondent) | @total × ((100 − @tax_rate) / 100) | 
| Remove a fixed tax % from a total (e.g. always 16% VAT) | @total × ((100 + 16) / 100) | 
| Calculate a quiz score | @score_q1  + @score_q2  + @score_q3 | 
| Build a URL with text concatenation | "https://example.com/"  + @page | 
| Combine first and last name | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name | 
| Prefix a field with a label | "ORD-"  + @order_id | 
| Build an address string | @street  + ", "  + @city  + ", "  + @country | 
| Make a certificate-style text | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name  + " has completed "  + @course_name | 
Tips:
- Always use @ + autocomplete to insert a form field
- Only type manually if you want to add text or numbers that aren’t collected in the form
- Use parentheses () to control order of operations
- Wrap literal text in double quotes, e.g. "https://example.com/" + @page
Calculations on date blocks are not available yet. 
By default, calculated values are not visible in your form. You can find them in the 
Submissions tab of your form, but you can also display the calculated values in your form, use them in a payment form, or create a dynamic redirect on completion.
To mention the calculated value in your form, simply type 
@ and choose the calculated field from the dropdown menu. You can use this to show a final price, score or quiz result in your form.
If you want to calculate and display currency, add your currency symbol directly before the linked calculated field, like in the example below.
You can use a calculated field to calculate the price of your payment form and make it dynamic based on your respondents’ answers. This means the price will change based on other inputs and logic.
- Type /payment to insert a payment form.
- Choose your calculated field from the Price dropdown menu in your payment block.
- The price will now automatically update according to your respondent's answers, for example, if they select different product types or quantities.
You can redirect respondents to different websites, landing pages, or Tally forms upon form completion. For this, you’ll need to use calculated fields and conditional logic.
You can also add hidden blocks to allow respondents to enter additional information before leaving the form for more comprehensive and trackable lead capture. As a result, the form creates an interactive landing page-like experience. 
You can use calculated fields to customize the email body or recipients of your respondent or self email notifications. Learn more about dynamic email notifications here.
Can I build a calculator with Tally?
Yes, use calculated fields together with conditional logic to build pricing calculators, quiz score counters, lead scoring systems, and more. Calculated fields are free for all users.
What's the difference between numeric operations and formulas?
Numeric operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) apply one step at a time via conditional logic. Formulas lets you write a single expression combining multiple operations, e.g. 
(price * quantity) - discount.
Can calculated fields be hidden from respondents?
Yes. Calculated fields and conditional logic are only visible to you in the form editor. Respondents only see them if you explicitly 
@ mention the field value somewhere in the form.
I want to display the result on the Thank You page
Use answer piping: type 
@ on your Thank You page and select the calculated field from the dropdown. The respondent will see the final value after submission.
My calculated field always shows 0
This is almost always a placement or logic ordering issue. Check the following:
- The calculated field must be placed BELOW the questions it references. Tally evaluates fields top-to-bottom. If your calculated field appears above a question it references, it can't read that question's value yet. Move the calculated field to after all questions that feed into it.
- Conditional logic must fire before the calculated field is displayed. If you're using conditional logic to show/hide questions, make sure the logic conditions are evaluated before the calculated field block appears in the form flow.
- Test in the published form, not the editor. The editor preview doesn't always reflect real-time calculation. Publish your form (or use the preview link) to see the actual calculated result.
- Check your formula for typos. Field references are case-sensitive. Open the calculated field and confirm each @FieldName matches exactly the question title in your form.

Visualize answers as charts, get automatic NPS and CSAT scores, track visits and traffic sources, and see where respondents drop off, all from the 
Insights tab.
✔️ Visualize answers with charts
✔️ Measure NPS & CSAT automatically
✔️ Track key metrics
✔️ Analyze friction points
Answer insights in Tally is completely free to use.
Open any published form and click 
Insights to visualize your form responses as charts, averages, and automatic scores. For multiple choice, checkboxes, dropdown, and multi-select questions, you'll see a bar chart by default, or switch to a pie chart with one click. The top answers are shown directly, with the rest grouped as Other, hover and click See all to expand the full list.
NPS and CSAT scores
Linear scale questions with a 0–10 range automatically get an NPS score, and 5-star rating questions automatically get a CSAT score, calculated from your responses so you can track sentiment at a glance. 
The 
Visits tab shows how many people are landing on your form and where they’re coming from, giving you a clear view of your reach and audience behavior.
What you’ll see:
- Visits: The total number of times your form has been viewed.
- Submissions: The number of submitted responses.
- Unique respondents: The number of unique respondents who submitted your form.
- Median visit duration: The median time respondents spent on your form, whether or not they submitted it.
- Time-based activity graphs: Graphs showing visits and submissions over time.
Traffic breakdown:
- Traffic sources: Where visitors came from (e.g. direct, search engines, referrals).
- Devices: Desktop, mobile, or tablet.
- Locations: Countries and cities where your visitors are based.
- Browsers: Which browsers your audience is using.
- Operating systems: Platforms like Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android.
Our analytics system uses data aggregation for time frames longer than 7 days, which can reduce accuracy across all visit metrics. This can lead to missing or inconsistent details compared to shorter time frames, like the last 7 days.
The 
Question drop-off tab helps you understand where users leave your form, so you can identify friction points and improve completion rates.
Here’s what you’ll find:
- Started answering: How many respondents began filling out the form.
- Completions: How many respondents successfully submitted the form.
- Completion rate: The percentage of form viewers who completed it.
- Completion duration: The median time it took respondents to complete the form.
Below the summary stats, you’ll see a step-by-step breakdown of your form questions, including:
- Views per question: How many respondents reached each question.
- Answer count: How many respondents responded to that question.
- Drop-off rate: The percentage and number of respondents who abandoned the form at that step.
What is a drop-off?
A drop-off is counted when someone starts filling out your form but leaves before completing it. The drop-off is attributed to the last question they were on when they left — think of it as "where in the form they got stuck." People who view your form but never interact with it are not counted in drop-off stats.
How is the drop-off rate calculated?
It's the percentage of respondents who started your form, reached that question, and left without completing the form.
A high drop-off rate may indicate confusion, friction, or lack of relevance. If you notice respondents are abandoning your form at a specific point, try these strategies to keep them moving forward:
🧠 Make questions easier to answer
- Rephrase long or complex questions for clarity.
- Mix question types to avoid repetition — alternate between open text and predefined choices.
- Reduce the number of required fields to lower the effort.
🎯 Keep it relevant and focused
- Use conditional logic to show only questions that matter to each respondent.
- Move sensitive or optional questions toward the end of the form.
- Split longer forms into multiple pages or steps to reduce overwhelm.
✨ Improve the user experience
- Enable the progress bar so respondents know how far they’ve come.
- Use engaging copy that feels conversational and welcoming.
- Design an attractive, user-friendly form.

Webhooks are available for free to all Tally users. 
If you're instead looking for a non-technical way to sync Tally form submissions with other apps, check out our Zapier, Make, Pipedream or Integrately integrations. If you’re building with AI agents or tools like Claude, check out the Tally MCP server. No endpoints or JSON required.
Webhooks send notifications to a specified URL when triggered by an event. The event trigger is a new form submission. When someone submits a Tally form, a notification containing the response data gets sent to your URL in JSON format via a POST request.
Publish your form and go to the 
Integrations tab. Click Connect to Webhooks.
You’ll be prompted to configure your webhook endpoint. 
For the endpoint URL, set up an HTTP or HTTPS endpoint that can accept webhook requests with a POST method:
- Handles POST requests with a JSON payload
- Returns a successful status code (2XX) within 10 seconds
A webhook endpoint has a 10-second timeout to process and respond to a new submission. If the processing takes longer, it's advisable to call another service internally. 
This enables the endpoint to swiftly send a successful status code to Tally. The separate service can then handle the processing of the submission without delaying the webhook response.
You can secure your webhook by using a signing secret to verify that Tally generated a webhook request and that it didn’t come from a server acting like Tally.
When this option is enabled, the webhook requests will contain a 
Tally-Signature header. The value of this header is a SHA256 cryptographic hash of the webhook payload. Express.js example
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.post('/webhook', (req, res) => {
  const webhookPayload = req.body;
  const receivedSignature = req.headers['tally-signature'];
  // Replace 'YOUR_SIGNING_SECRET' with your signing secret
  const yourSigningSecret = 'YOUR_SIGNING_SECRET';
  // Calculate the signature using the signing secret and the payload
  const calculatedSignature = createHmac('sha256', yourSigningSecret)
    .update(JSON.stringify(webhookPayload))
    .digest('base64');
  // Compare the received signature with the calculated signature
  if (receivedSignature === calculatedSignature) {
    // Signature is valid, process the webhook payload
    res.status(200).send('Webhook received and processed successfully.');
  } else {
    // Signature is invalid, reject the webhook request
    res.status(401).send('Invalid signature.');
  }
});
app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Server is running on port 3000'));
You can optionally configure custom HTTP headers that will be sent with each webhook request. Click 
Add HTTP headers and enter the header name and value. If a webhook endpoint fails to return a successful status code (2XX) within a 10-second window, we employ a retry mechanism to attempt delivery of the submission. Here is the sequence of retries:
- The first retry occurs after 5 minutes
- If the first retry fails, the second retry is scheduled after 30 minutes
- If the second retry fails, the third retry is scheduled after 1 hour
- If the third retry fails, the fourth retry is scheduled after 6 hours
- If the fourth retry fails, the fifth retry is scheduled after 1 day
If all retries fail, we'll also send a one-time email to the form owner and creator with the reason and a link to fix it. We won't email again for the same failure until it resolves and happens again.
You will see the active webhook URLs in your published form dashboard. You can connect unlimited webhook URLs and pause them by clicking the toggle.

For free, and without login.","content":"A file upload form lets you collect files directly from respondents, without the need for them to sign up. With Tally, you can add a file upload field to any form and start collecting images, PDFs, videos, audio files, and documents in minutes. You can allow multiple file uploads, define the file types and set size limits to match your needs. File upload forms are free on all Tally plans, with no limit on the number of files you can collect.

If you want respondents to be able to upload multiple files, enable the 
Multiple files option. This will allow you to define the desired minimum and maximum number of file uploads.

Upload another file button.
Enable 
Max file size to set a file size limit. Respondents will see the maximum file size limit in the file upload block.
To only accept certain file types, enable 
Allowed files and select the file type(s) you want to accept. For example: - If you only want to accept image files, regardless of the type, select All image files

Collect credit card payments securely via Stripe, with no coding required and no extra fees added on top ever.","content":"Looking for a quick and simple way to sell products online? With Tally, you can build payment forms in minutes and collect credit card payments without a single line of code.
Stripe is a payment processing platform that allows individuals and businesses to send and receive payments over the Internet. It provides a secure and easy-to-use interface for managing transactions, with many businesses using it for online payments. Tally integrates with Stripe to enable users to collect credit card payments through our forms.
All standard Stripe fees apply when using our Stripe Connect integration. This includes processing fees for payments, currency conversions (if applicable), and any additional charges set by Stripe based on your account or country. We do not add any extra fees on top of Stripe’s pricing.
Type 
/payment to insert the payment block.
Enter the price by simply typing the amount (or choose a calculated price or any other variable from the dropdown menu) and the currency of your product. If you don't find the currency you want, don't hesitate to contact us.

Connect with Stripe. If you are new to Stripe, you need to create a (free) Stripe account before you can connect your payment form.
In your published form, your respondents will see a secure payment view where they can enter their credit card details to pay for your product or service.
Payments are processed if your respondent clicks the 
Next or Submit button in your form.
When the payment is processed and the respondent returns to a previous page in the form, you will see the payment status 
Payment received in the form.
The payment data will be available both in Tally and in Stripe. Tally does not store credit card details for security reasons. 
You’ll find the total amount of collected payments per form in your dashboard.
The payment details of each respondent are available in your Tally form 
Submissions and Summary tab. In the Summary tab, click the ↗️ icon to open payments in Stripe.
In Stripe, you will see the payment and the form name in your Payments tab. Your form title will show in the Description tab.
With Tally's calculated fields, you can calculate a price and update your payment form in real time based on your respondents’ answers. You could use this to:
- Automatically calculate and update the price in your payment form
- Create a shopping basket on a checkout page
- Calculate shipping costs
Can I test payments?
It is not possible yet to use Stripe’s test cards to test the payment form, but you can upvote this feature here.
Can I create receipts or invoices for collected payments?
Our Stripe integration automatically sends a receipt to the email address specified by your respondent. It does not automatically generate invoices. Stripe provides options to generate and send invoices after payment.
Can I collect recurring payments?
We don’t support collecting recurring payments. 
How do I change the price?
It’s not possible to change the price of the payment block. You can set a new price by removing the payment block and creating a new one, following the process described in this article.
If you want to be able to easily change the price, you can use a calculated field as input in your payment block. This helps prevent duplicate submissions, resulting in much cleaner, more accurate, reliable data.","content":"You can enable a toggle in your form settings to ensure each respondent submits your form only once. This helps prevent duplicate submissions, resulting in more accurate and reliable data.
Preventing duplicate submissions is a free feature available to all Tally users. 
After publishing your form, turn on the 
Prevent duplicate submissions toggle in your form settings. The setting is in the Access section.
Select a unique identifier field (such as IP address, email, Respondent ID or any other form field), which Tally will use to detect and prevent duplicate submissions. 
Whenever Tally detects a duplicate submission attempt, the respondent will see this error page pop up, preventing them from submitting the form.
You have a registration form with an email input field, and you select it as the unique identifier.
The error page will pop up when someone tries to submit the form again using the same email. The error message uses Tally default form text, which means if you change form language, it will also apply to the error message.
You can use any form field as the unique identifier, such as an input field, hidden field, calculated field, IP address, and Respondent ID. You’ll see all available fields for your form when you click the dropdown. Not all options are 100% bulletproof, but each helps deter spam in its own way.
An IP address is a unique string of numbers that identifies each computer on the Internet. It functions as an address that allows data to be sent and received between devices on a network. 
People in the same company or school often have the same IP address when connected to the same internal network because organizations usually use a shared public IP address for all devices connected to their network. In such a situation, using an IP address to prevent duplicate submissions would restrict other respondents on the same network from filling in your form.
Respondents can avoid being detected by using different networks. For example, they can switch from home Wi-Fi to mobile data or use a VPN, which changes their IP address.
The Respondent ID is a Universally Unique Identifier (UUID v4), a string of random numbers automatically assigned to every new respondent. It doesn't contain information other than a random string of numbers. The Respondent ID is stored on the respondent's browser (local storage), and if they submit another response, Tally can block it.
Respondents can bypass this check using a different browser or device (e.g., desktop vs. phone), or Incognito mode.
You can pick any input field (such as email, phone, name) as a unique identifier, as well as hidden or calculated fields.
Respondents can bypass this check by entering any type of content they want. For example, a respondent can enter an email address that is not theirs. 
If you turn on the 
Verify email toggle in the Email block, respondents must verify their email before proceeding. Learn more about Email verification.
Can I customize the error message when a respondent’s submission is denied?
No, at the moment, it is a default message. However, if you change the form language, the error message will also be translated.
Does the duplicate prevention feature take into account submissions before enabling it?
No. Only submissions made after enabling the feature are considered for duplicate prevention.
Does Tally support IP address collection upon form submission?
No, currently we don’t collect IP addresses.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_0ad9b62d7a96f94c3989","url":"https://tally.so/help/recaptcha","title":"Block Spam with reCAPTCHA | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Add Google reCAPTCHA to your Tally forms to block spam and bots, while keeping forms fast and easy for real users to submit. A complete step-by-step guide to managing and restoring your form responses.","content":"Whether you're clearing test entries or staying compliant with data privacy regulations, Tally lets you easily delete forms, workspaces, and form submission data. Deleted items are stored in Trash for 90 days before they're permanently deleted, giving you time to restore anything deleted by mistake.
Every item (forms, submissions or workspaces) you delete in Tally goes to Trash first. 
Nothing is permanently removed until you explicitly 
Empty trash, or 90 days pass.
Once an item is permanently deleted (either by you or after 90 days), it cannot be recovered.
Click 
… next to your form or workspace in the sidebar or dashboard and Delete.
Deleting a workspace will also delete all forms within that workspace. Deleting a form will also delete all form submissions of that form.
Go to the 
submissions tab of your published form, select one or multiple entries and click the trash icon 🗑️.
You can restore any form, workspace, or submission from Trash within the 90-day window.
- Click the Trash icon in the left sidebar.
- Find the item you want to restore.
- Click the ↺ (restore) icon next to it.
The item returns to its original location with all settings, submissions, and integrations intact.
How long are deleted items kept in Trash?
Deleted forms, workspaces, and submissions are kept in Trash for 90 days. After that, Tally removes them permanently and automatically.
Can I recover a permanently deleted form?
No. Once an item is permanently deleted, either by emptying the Trash or after 90 days, it cannot be recovered. Always double-check before permanently deleting.
What happens to a form's public URL after I delete it?
The form becomes inaccessible at its public URL as soon as it's moved to Trash. Visitors will see an error page.
Can I set a form to auto-delete submissions automatically?
Yes. You can set a custom retention period for each form — from minutes up to years. # Tally Help Center

> Practical help for creating, publishing, and improving Tally forms, from first-form tutorials to logic, integrations, and submission management.

Tally’s editor works like a document: type to build a form, or use a template instead of starting from scratch.

Tally offers unlimited forms and submissions on its free plan, subject to its fair use policy. Some settings, including partial submissions, require a paid plan.

## Create your form

- [Create your first form](<https://tally.so/help/create-a-form>): Build questions, customize the form, then publish and share it.
- [Use a form template](<https://tally.so/help/form-templates>): Start with a ready-made template, customize it, or save a form as a reusable template.
- [Choose input blocks](<https://tally.so/help/input-blocks>): Compare question and input types, including choices, dates, files, and payments.
- [Create a multi-page form](<https://tally.so/help/how-to-create-a-multi-step-form>): Add page breaks, group questions, and set up one-question-per-page flows.
- [Customize your form](<https://tally.so/help/customize-your-form>): Adjust themes, fonts, images, layout, and other design options.

## Add logic and personalize responses

- [Conditional logic](<https://tally.so/help/conditional-form-logic>): Show or hide blocks, jump between pages, calculate values, and troubleshoot rules.
- [Calculated fields](<https://tally.so/help/form-calculator>): Calculate scores or prices from answers and display or use the results.
- [Hidden fields](<https://tally.so/help/hidden-fields>): Pass values through URL parameters to track sources or prefill information.
- [Answer piping](<https://tally.so/help/answer-piping>): Insert earlier answers into later questions, text, or thank-you messages.
- [Thank You pages](<https://tally.so/help/how-to-create-a-thank-you-page>): Customize the message after submission or use different pages for different logic paths.
- [Form settings](<https://tally.so/help/form-settings>): Configure access, notifications, language, respondent behavior, and other published-form settings.

## Publish and share

- [Embed a form](<https://tally.so/help/embed-your-form>): Add a standard, popup, or full-page form embed to a website.
- [Set up a popup form](<https://tally.so/help/popup-forms>): Choose a popup trigger and appearance, then add its code to your site.
- [Redirect after submission](<https://tally.so/help/redirect-on-completion>): Send respondents to another URL, optionally using form data or conditional logic.
- [Collect payments](<https://tally.so/help/payment-forms>): Connect a payment block to Stripe; standard Stripe fees apply, and recurring payments are not supported.

## Connect submissions to other tools

- [Browse integrations](<https://tally.so/help/integrations>): Find direct integrations, automation tools, webhooks, and developer options.
- [Google Sheets integration](<https://tally.so/help/google-sheets-integration>): Send submissions to a spreadsheet and check sync logs if entries are missing.
- [Notion integration](<https://tally.so/help/notion-integration>): Map form fields to Notion database properties and troubleshoot connection or sync issues.
- [Webhooks](<https://tally.so/help/webhooks>): Send submission data to an endpoint and inspect delivery events.
- [Tally API](<https://tally.so/help/api>): Create and manage forms or submissions programmatically; includes authentication and rate-limit guidance.

## Review results and fix problems

- [Form Insights](<https://tally.so/help/form-insights>): Review response charts and visit metrics; question drop-off insights require Pro.
- [Partial submissions](<https://tally.so/help/partial-submissions>): Set up Pro-only capture of unfinished responses and understand its export and integration limits.
- [Prevent duplicate submissions](<https://tally.so/help/prevent-duplicate-submissions>): Choose an identifier to deter repeat entries and understand where each option can be bypassed.
- [Add reCAPTCHA](<https://tally.so/help/recaptcha>): Place a spam-protection block near Submit, particularly on multi-page forms.
- [Delete and recover form data](<https://tally.so/help/how-to-delete-and-recover-form-data>): Restore deleted forms or submissions from Trash within 90 days, before permanent deletion.
- [Restore a form version](<https://tally.so/help/form-version-history>): Preview and restore a saved version; republish to update an already-live form.
- [Frequently asked questions](<https://tally.so/help/faq>): Find quick answers about exports, saved answers, embeds, and common form behavior.

## Plan and responsible-use details

- [Plans and feature availability](<https://tally.so/help/plans-and-pricing>): Check how Tally describes its free, Pro, and Business offerings.
- [Fair use policy](<https://tally.so/help/fair-use-policy>): Review usage thresholds and the policy for sustained high-volume activity.
- [Build accessible forms](<https://tally.so/help/accessibility>): Follow form-content guidance and review stated accessibility limitations before publishing.
- [GDPR information](<https://tally.so/help/gdpr>): Read Tally’s account of its data practices and the form creator’s responsibilities; not legal advice.
